title: Optimistic Updates
readme:
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

This package contains 13 focused lesson PDFs, one combined book, and a TaskFlow reference snapshot.

Core architecture: UI optimism where one component needs the prediction; cache optimism only where multiple observers need shared pending state; rollback on rejection; server reconciliation through targeted invalidation.

lessons.title: Optimistic UI Mental Model and When to Use It
lessons.summary: Optimistic UI Mental Model and When to Use It Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture What optimistic means The user performs an action and TaskFlow immediately renders the result it expects the server to accept. The HTTP request still happens.…
lessons.body:
Optimistic UI Mental Model and When
to Use It
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

What optimistic means
The user performs an action and TaskFlow immediately renders the result it expects the server to
accept. The HTTP request still happens. If the backend rejects the operation, the UI must recover.

Good candidates
• Low-risk reversible changes such as toggling a Task status when the transition is usually
accepted.

• Edits with predictable local results and small payloads.

• Actions where immediate feedback materially improves perceived responsiveness.

• Operations with a clear rollback path.

Poor candidates
• Payments, payroll finalization, destructive bulk actions, or irreversible approvals.

• Operations where the server calculates an unpredictable result.

• Actions likely to fail due to permissions or complex business rules.

• Writes where pretending success would mislead the user materially.

Decision rule
Optimistic UX should reduce waiting without creating false confidence. For sensitive workflows, a
visible pending state is often better than pretending completion.

lessons.title: UI Optimism with Mutation Variables
lessons.summary: UI Optimism with Mutation Variables Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Start with the simpler strategy Two optimistic strategies in TanStack Query UI optimism Cache optimism Render mutation.variables while pending onMutate changes cached data No cache rewrite Snapshot + rollback…
lessons.body:
UI Optimism with Mutation Variables
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Start with the simpler strategy
Two optimistic strategies in TanStack Query

UI optimism                                               Cache optimism
Render mutation.variables while pending                          onMutate changes cached data
No cache rewrite                                       Snapshot + rollback required
Simpler rollback story                                 Useful across multiple consumers

Default to UI optimism when one place needs the prediction.

Use cache optimism when several observers must see the same pending change.

TanStack Query supports rendering the pending mutation variables directly. This changes what the
user sees without modifying the Query cache. That means there is no cache snapshot to restore.

Status button example
const updateStatus = useMutation({
mutationKey: ["tasks", "update-status", task.id],
mutationFn: (status: TaskStatus) =>
updateTask(task.id, { status }),
onSettled: () =>
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
queryKey: taskKeys.all,
}),
})

const visibleStatus =
updateStatus.isPending
? updateStatus.variables
: task.status

Why this is powerful
• The original Query cache remains untouched.

• A failure naturally falls back to the cached server value.

• The mutation can still expose an inline error and retry action.

• This is ideal when only the component initiating the mutation needs to render the prediction.

Cross-component pending UI
If another component must display the pending mutation, give the mutation a stable mutationKey
and read matching pending variables with useMutationState().

lessons.title: Query Cancellation and Stale Refetch Races
lessons.summary: Query Cancellation and Stale Refetch Races Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The race Why cancelQueries comes before the optimistic cache write Time Refetch old server response Optimistic new predicted value stale refetch can overwrite prediction cancelQueries() prevents the in-flight…
lessons.body:
Query Cancellation and Stale Refetch
Races
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

The race
Why cancelQueries comes before the optimistic cache write

Time

Refetch                                                                 old server response

Optimistic                                             new predicted value
stale refetch can overwrite prediction

cancelQueries() prevents the in-flight query from winning this race.

Why cancellation is before setQueryData
Suppose Task detail is refetching. You then optimistically change its status. If the older refetch
resolves a moment later, it can replace the optimistic value with stale server data. Calling
cancelQueries() first closes that race for the targeted query.

Cancellation is targeted
await queryClient.cancelQueries({
queryKey: taskKeys.detail(taskId),
})

Do not cancel the world
Cancel only queries whose in-flight results could overwrite the optimistic state you are about to
change. Broad cancellation creates unnecessary churn and can hide unrelated data refreshes.

lessons.title: Filtered and Paginated Caches
lessons.summary: Filtered and Paginated Caches Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The hard part is list membership One mutation can affect several cached views differently All Tasks status=TODO status=DONE Task remains visible Task may disappear Task may appear Perfectly recreating every…
lessons.body:
Filtered and Paginated Caches
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

The hard part is list membership
One mutation can affect several cached views differently

All Tasks                               status=TODO                               status=DONE
Task remains visible                      Task may disappear                          Task may appear

Perfectly recreating every filtered + paginated server result on the client is expensive.

Prefer a small local prediction, then invalidate and let the server reconcile authoritative lists.

Why “patch every list” becomes fragile
A status update can remove a Task from one filtered page, add it to another filter, shift page
boundaries, change counts, and interact with search/sort order. Reproducing all backend query
semantics in client cache code creates a second query engine that can drift from NestJS/Prisma
behavior.

TaskFlow strategy
• Use UI optimism for the visible row when possible.

• Optimistically patch the Task detail cache when several observers need the same pending value.

• Avoid fabricating pagination metadata.

• Invalidate list prefixes after settlement so the server reconstructs the authoritative collection.

• Only implement filter-aware list patching for specific high-value interactions with strong tests.

Important rule
If an optimistic cache algorithm starts reimplementing filtering, authorization, search, sorting, and
pagination, stop. You are duplicating backend responsibility.

lessons.title: Optimistic Create and Temporary Identity
lessons.summary: Optimistic Create and Temporary Identity Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Creating is different from updating An update already has a stable server identity. A create request may not. Inventing a fake database ID and inserting it into every cache…
lessons.body:
Optimistic Create and Temporary
Identity
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Creating is different from updating
An update already has a stable server identity. A create request may not. Inventing a fake database
ID and inserting it into every cache can create difficult reconciliation bugs.

Preferred first approach
For Task creation, TaskFlow initially uses UI optimism: render the pending mutation variables as a
temporary row while the request is pending, then invalidate the Task list when the server returns.

Mutation state across components
const pendingCreates = useMutationState({
filters: {
mutationKey: ["tasks", "create"],
status: "pending",
},
select: mutation => ({
input: mutation.state.variables,
submittedAt: mutation.state.submittedAt,
}),
})

Why submittedAt helps
Multiple creates can be pending simultaneously. submittedAt gives each pending mutation a
client-side rendering key without pretending it is the permanent Task ID.

When temporary IDs are justified
Offline-first applications, drag/drop composition before sync, or complex local graph editing may
justify a real client-generated temporary identity strategy. TaskFlow has not earned that complexity
yet.

lessons.summary: Concurrent Mutations and Mutation Scopes Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Mutations run in parallel by default Two rapid clicks can produce two independent update requests. If they target the same Task, response order may differ from intent order. That…
lessons.body:
Concurrent Mutations and Mutation
Scopes
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Mutations run in parallel by default
Two rapid clicks can produce two independent update requests. If they target the same Task,
response order may differ from intent order. That means a naive optimistic implementation can
show stale or surprising final state.

Serializing one Task status stream
const updateStatus = useMutation({
mutationKey: ["tasks", "status", taskId],
scope: {
id: `task-status:${taskId}`,
},
mutationFn: (status: TaskStatus) =>
updateTask(taskId, { status }),
// optimistic callbacks...
})

What scope does
TanStack Query documents that mutations run in parallel by default. Mutations with the same
scope.id execute serially, with later ones queued while an earlier one is running.

Do not serialize unrelated work
Different Tasks should normally remain independent. Use the smallest scope that matches the
resource/workflow whose ordering must be preserved.

Global pending indicators
Use useMutationState() or useIsMutating() with mutation keys for focused “Saving…” indicators
rather than a hand-built global boolean.

lessons.summary: Rollback, Error Semantics and Business Rejection Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Failure is part of the design An optimistic UI is incomplete until the learner can explain what happens for 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, network failure, and 500.…
lessons.body:
Rollback, Error Semantics and
Business Rejection
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Failure is part of the design
An optimistic UI is incomplete until the learner can explain what happens for 400, 401, 403, 404,
409, network failure, and 500.

TaskFlow behavior
400                            Rollback prediction; show field/input problem if the mutation came from a form.

401                            Rollback; recover authentication/session instead of blind retry.

403                            Rollback; explain that the authenticated user is not permitted.

409                            Rollback; surface the business conflict or invalid state transition.

5xx/network                    Rollback; preserve retry affordance and requestId when available.

Example business conflict
A user may optimistically click DONE, but NestJS can reject the transition because another
workflow changed the Task first. The rollback is not an exceptional edge case; it is normal
distributed-system behavior.

Never hide the rejection
Do not silently snap the UI back with no explanation. Roll back the data and communicate why the
optimistic prediction failed.

lessons.body:
Accessibility and Optimistic UX
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Instant does not mean invisible
Visual speed should not remove meaningful feedback. A status change that is still pending needs
an accessible representation so keyboard and assistive-technology users are not left guessing.

Good patterns
• Keep the control disabled only when duplicate intent would be harmful; otherwise allow
independent actions.

• Use visible “Saving…” or “Pending” text when the mutation materially changes state.

• Use aria-live="polite" for concise status messages when appropriate.

• Preserve focus after rollback; do not remount the entire table.

• Announce server rejection in a nearby error region rather than only changing color.

Avoid misleading success
Do not announce “Saved” at the moment of onMutate. At that point the UI has predicted success;
the server has not confirmed it.

lessons.body:
Testing, Debugging and Devtools
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

What to test
Optimistic code should be tested as a state machine, not only as a successful click.

Core matrix
• Mutation starts: predicted value appears immediately.

• In-flight refetch cannot overwrite the prediction.

• Successful response replaces prediction with server value.

• 400/403/409/network failure restores previous cache value.

• List queries invalidate after settlement.

• Two updates to the same Task preserve intended ordering when scoped serially.

• Two different Tasks can mutate independently.

• Pending create rows disappear after success and are replaced by server-backed query data.

• Filtered pages reconcile correctly after invalidation.

Devtools clues
• Watch the Task detail query before, during, and after onMutate.

• Inspect mutation status, variables, submittedAt, and mutationKey.

• Confirm invalidation marks only the intended query families stale.

• Look for duplicate refetches caused by both onSuccess and onSettled performing the same work.

Debugging rule
If the UI ends in the wrong state, write the timeline: previous cache -> onMutate -> request A/B ->
callback order -> invalidation -> refetch. Optimistic bugs are usually ordering bugs.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit
Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates

Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Lab 1 - UI optimism
Convert the Task status control to render mutation.variables while pending. Do not touch the
cache. Add an inline retry action on failure.

Lab 2 - Cache optimism
On a Task detail page, snapshot the Task query, cancel it, patch the status in onMutate, restore it in
onError, and replace it with the server response in onSuccess.

Lab 3 - Concurrency
Trigger multiple status changes quickly. First observe parallel behavior. Then add a per-Task
mutation scope and verify the queue preserves ordering for that Task while other Tasks remain
independent.

Lab 4 - Failure drills
• Force a 403 and confirm rollback + explanation.

• Force a 409 state-transition conflict and confirm rollback.

• Throttle/offline the network and observe pending UI and retry behavior.

• Keep a Task list filtered by status and verify the authoritative list after invalidation.

Exit criteria
• I can explain UI optimism versus cache optimism.

• I can implement cancel -> snapshot -> patch -> rollback -> reconcile.

• I understand why list caches are harder than detail caches.

• I can reason about multiple concurrent mutations.

• I know which high-risk operations should remain pessimistic.

• I can debug an optimistic race with a timeline rather than guessing.

https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework   through mutation variables and cache optimism through

https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework   before an optimistic cache write that could otherwise be
/react/guides/query-cancellation                   overwritten by an in-flight refetch.

Source                                              Use in this phase

Mutations                                           and awaiting invalidation when pending state should include
https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework    reconciliation.

https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework    default, while identical scope IDs serialize execution.
/react/guides/mutations

https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework    supports concurrent optimistic UI with mutation keys and
/react/reference/functions/useMutationState         submittedAt.

TanStack Query - QueryClient                        Documents get/setQueryData, cancelQueries,
https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/reference/   invalidateQueries, getQueriesData, setQueriesData, and
QueryClient                                         cache control used by optimistic workflows.

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 25: Optimistic Updates

Purpose
Add optimistic UI safely by defining snapshot, optimistic state, rollback, reconciliation, temporary identity, and concurrency behavior.

Deliverable
Optimistic task update/create flow with rollback and authoritative server reconciliation.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
user action -> cancel/snapshot relevant queries -> optimistic cache write -> server mutation -> rollback on error -> invalidate/reconcile on settle

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Choose one mutation where low failure probability and UX benefit justify optimism.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Capture the previous cache state before changing it.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Apply an optimistic update to the exact affected query data.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Force a server failure and prove rollback restores the previous state.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — On success/settle, reconcile with authoritative server data rather than trusting the optimistic object forever.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Simulate two rapid mutations and reason about race ordering and stale responses.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 25: Optimistic Updates

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
user action -> cancel/snapshot relevant queries -> optimistic cache write -> server mutation -> rollback on error -> invalidate/reconcile on settle

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Optimism without rollback
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Temporary IDs colliding with real IDs
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Older mutation response overwriting newer user intent
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Optimistically updating the wrong filtered list
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Optimistic Updates

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 25 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Add optimistic UI safely by defining snapshot, optimistic state, rollback, reconciliation, temporary identity, and concurrency behavior.

Required artifact
Optimistic task update/create flow with rollback and authoritative server reconciliation.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can implement snapshot/rollback/reconcile.
• Can decide when optimism is inappropriate.
• Can handle temporary identity.
• Can reason about concurrent mutations.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose one mutation where low failure probability and UX benefit justify optimism.
2. Capture the previous cache state before changing it.
3. Apply an optimistic update to the exact affected query data.
4. Force a server failure and prove rollback restores the previous state.
5. On success/settle, reconcile with authoritative server data rather than trusting the optimistic object forever.
6. Simulate two rapid mutations and reason about race ordering and stale responses.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 25: Optimistic Updates. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Optimistic task update/create flow with rollback and authoritative server reconciliation.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

references.preview:
# Optimistic Update Decision Table

| Operation | Course decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Task status toggle | Optimistic | Small, reversible, predictable result |
| Task title edit | Usually optimistic | Predictable, but preserve server validation errors |
| Create Task | UI optimism first | Avoid inventing fake permanent IDs |
| Delete Task | Usually pessimistic initially | Destructive; accidental false success is costly |
| Membership role change | Pessimistic | Security-sensitive authorization operation |
| Payroll finalization | Pessimistic | High-impact irreversible business workflow |
| Purchase-order approval | Usually pessimistic | Approval rules may fail and user should not see false completion |

# TaskFlow Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Snapshot

This snapshot extends the Phase 22 TanStack Query architecture. It intentionally demonstrates two strategies:

1. UI optimism through mutation variables (preferred when one view needs the prediction).
2. Cache optimism through onMutate + rollback (used when several observers share the same Task detail cache).

The server remains authoritative. Task list caches are invalidated after settlement rather than attempting to reproduce every filter/pagination rule in client code.

# Phase 25 Optimistic Update Test Matrix

| Scenario | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Status mutation starts | Predicted status appears immediately |
| Detail query is refetching | cancelQueries prevents stale response from overwriting prediction |
| Server accepts status | Detail cache uses server Task; lists invalidate |
| Server returns 403 | Previous Task detail is restored; permission error shown |
| Server returns 409 | Previous Task detail is restored; conflict explained |
| Network fails | Previous Task detail is restored; retry remains possible |
| Two changes same Task | Same scope serializes requests in intent order |
| Two changes different Tasks | Requests can run independently |
| Create Task pending | Temporary UI row uses mutation variables + submittedAt |
| Create succeeds | Pending row disappears after list refetch returns server Task |
| Status-filtered list | List is reconciled by invalidation/refetch rather than fabricated client metadata |
| Logout while mutations exist | Existing Phase 22 logout clears QueryClient cache |
